results.title: Professor Jyoti Choudhary
results.content: Professor Jyoti Choudhary's research focuses on understanding how the organisation and dynamics of protein networks underpin cancer progression and resistance. She also investigates the impact of mutations and genetic variation on the proteome and protein attributes using quantitative mass spectrometry. She joined the Bioanalytical Sciences division in GlaxoWellcome as a senior scientist and was subsequently selected as a group leader in the CellMap project - a technology incubator unit founded to pursue the development of cutting edge proteomics technologies for drug discovery applications. Her group implemented endogenous gene tagging, eTAP, in mouse stem cells and applied it to systematically study native protein complexes in a range of cell types and tissues. These were then used to refine annotation of the mammalian and malaria genomes, as well as to study the impact of genetic variation on protein networks.

Structural and biochemical analysis of family 92 carbohydrate-binding modules uncovers multivalent binding to β-glucans. Carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) are non-catalytic proteins found appended to carbohydrate-active enzymes. We present crystal structures for two proteins, and confirm by mutagenesis that tryptophan residues permit ligand binding at three distinct functional binding sites on each protein. Carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) are low molecular weight, non-catalytic protein domains that bind carbohydrate ligands, and are classified by sequence homology into families on the carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy) database (www.cazy.org)1 in 2013. However, the first apparent demonstration in the literature of carbohydrate binding by a CBM92 protein appears to be the β−1,3-glucanase LamC from a myxobacterial *Corallococcus* species, where affinity gel electrophoresis showed that a BFLD at the N-terminus of a GH16 catalytic domain could bind to β−1,3-glucans11-glucanase from Corallococcus sp.

results.title: Howard Y. Chang, MD, PhD's Profile | Stanford Profiles
results.content: My research has focused on mechanisms that coordinate the activities of large number of genes in cell fate control. We made a series of discoveries that introduced the important and pervasive roles of long noncoding RNAs in biological regulation. My group has substantial experience in epigenetics and RNA biology, including invention of new methods for epigenomic profiling, map RNA occupancy on chromatin, and define RNA structures genome-wide. My group pioneered methods to identify key regulators of large-scale transcriptional programs; these methods have been highly fruitful for studies of development, cancer, and aging. The long term goal of my laboratory is to decipher the regulatory information in the human genome for disease diagnosis and therapy. This has enabled the creation of faithful laboratory models of human cancer types, identified specific drugs that can target these cancers, and revealed the hierarchy of transcriptional programs involved in the generation of cancer stem cellsthe cells that continually repopulate a tumor or its metastases.

results.content: # How do fundamental groups shape our... ## Università Bocconi's Post. ### **Università Bocconi**. How do fundamental groups shape our understanding of mathematical structures? We are proud to announce that Elia Bruè, from Bocconi’s Department of Decision Sciences, has been honored with the Frontiers of Science Award 2025 for his outstanding research in topology, a branch of mathematics that explores the fundamental properties of geometric objects. The award-winning paper, "Fundamental Groups and the Milnor Conjecture," co-authored with Aaron Naber (Institute of Advanced Studies, Princeton University) and Daniele Semola (Swiss Federal Polytechnic, Zurich), presents groundbreaking insights into fundamental groups and Milnor’s Conjecture, opening new perspectives on one of the most captivating topics in contemporary mathematics. As part of this honor, Bruè, Naber, and Semola have been invited to Beijing in July 2025 to attend the official award ceremony, where they will present their findings to an audience of leading scientists from around the world. This recognition is a testament to the research conducted at Bocconi, and we are thrilled to celebrate our faculty’s contributions to advancing knowledge in fundamental sciences.
